Strategies for Gastroenterologists to Reduce the Burden of Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer Within Their Communities
  • Source: American Journal of Gastroenterology, Vol. XX, Issue XX
  • Topic: Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer (EOCRC) Prevention and Screening Strategies
  • Author(s): Mahmoud T, Hasan S, Yoshida C (University of Virginia Health System)
  • Word Count: 1,428
EOCRC Crisis Overview
  • Global incidence --> 3% annually
  • Leading cause of cancer-related deaths among adults <50 years
  • Individuals born in 1990s have ~3x risk of CRC vs those born in 1950s
  • Individuals <50 years --> nearly 16% of new CRC cases
EOCRC Risk Factors
  • 14–34% of EOCRC patients have family history of CRC
  • 16–20% have identifiable germline mutations
  • Most EOCRC --> sporadic disease driven by environmental/lifestyle exposures
Strategy 1: Family Risk Communication
  • First-degree relatives (FDRs) of CRC/advanced colorectal polyp (ACP) patients have ~2x lifetime risk vs general population
  • US Multi-Society Task Force (USMSTF) recommends:
  • Screening beginning at age 40
  • OR 10 years younger than earliest CRC/ACP diagnosis in family
  • Communication of familial risk --> inconsistent in practice
Practical Implementation Tools
Endoscopy Report/Colonoscopy Discharge Materials
  • Template: "You were found to have an advanced precancerous polyp. Please inform your first-degree relatives as they may need to begin colon cancer screening at age 40 or 10 years earlier than your diagnosis."
  • Auto-populate for relevant pathology results
Pathology Follow-Up Letter
  • Template: "Because advanced polyps can run in families, your parents, siblings, and children should discuss earlier colonoscopy (before age 45) with their physician."
  • Provide bilingual versions when possible
Patient Portal Message
  • Template: "Your results suggest an increased familial risk. Share this message with close family so they can benefit from earlier screening."
Workflow Strategies
  • Integrate templated communication tools into EHR (e.g., Epic smartphrases)
  • Collaborate with primary care providers to document family history of CRC/ACP
  • Ensure accurate EHR documentation --> facilitates "on-time" screening for at-risk FDRs
Strategy 2: Timely Colonoscopy After Positive Stool-Based Test
  • Stool-based tests (SBTs) use --> increased substantially during/after COVID-19 pandemic
  • SBTs preferred by young adults due to lower cost and greater convenience vs colonoscopy
  • Two-step process: positive SBT requires diagnostic colonoscopy to complete screening continuum
Critical Timing Data
  • Delays beyond 6 months associated with:
  • ↑ CRC incidence
  • More advanced stage at diagnosis
  • ↑ CRC-related mortality
  • Only 48% of patients with abnormal SBT receive follow-up colonoscopy within 6 months
Quality Measure Target
  • Proposed measure: 80% completion of follow-up colonoscopy within 6 months of positive SBT
  • Achieving 80% uptake --> could prevent 280,000 new CRC cases
  • Could avert 200,000 cancer deaths by 2030
Practical Strategies
  • Prioritize positive SBT referrals
  • Designate abnormal SBT results as "Tier 1" to expedite scheduling
  • Strengthen referral pathways:
  • Ensure referrals clearly labeled as positive SBT
  • Reserve dedicated colonoscopy slots for high-risk patients
  • Allow direct scheduling for positive SBT cases
  • Adopt proposed quality measure:
  • Implement EHR/practice-level database monitoring systems
  • Regularly review performance metrics
  • Refine scheduling workflows when targets not met
Strategy 3: Prioritize Colonoscopy for Symptomatic Young Patients
  • Substantial diagnostic delays: 4–6 months between initial symptoms and diagnosis
  • Young patients more likely to present with late-stage disease vs older counterparts
Red-Flag Symptoms (Alarm Features)
  • Rectal bleeding
  • Persistent bowel habit change
  • Abdominal pain
  • Unexplained iron deficiency anemia
Scheduling Strategies
  • Establish "Red-flag"/"Tier 1" scheduling status for symptomatic patients <50 years
  • Define alarm features triggering expedited referral
  • Goal: Colonoscopy within 90 days of referral for symptomatic patients
  • Use EMR alerts to flag symptomatic young patients
  • Track referral-to-colonoscopy intervals
Strategy 4: Social Media for EOCRC Awareness
  • Low awareness of EOCRC among young adults --> persistent barrier to timely diagnosis
  • Social media --> powerful tool for reaching younger populations
Campaign Benefits
  • ↑ awareness of red-flag symptoms
  • Normalize conversations about bowel health
  • Highlight risk factors for disease
  • Empower young people to adopt preventive healthy lifestyle habits
  • Create community and prevent isolation for EOCRC survivors
Social Media Content Analysis (TikTok)
  • Videos garnered millions of views and widespread engagement
  • Few videos created by healthcare professionals
  • Overall educational quality --> limited
  • Gap: Clinicians need more active role in shaping accurate, accessible online content
Evidence Limitations
  • Social media campaigns show measurable improvements in public awareness and screening behaviors (#CRCandMe campaign)
  • Evidence linking campaigns to behavioral changes and direct clinical outcomes (screening completion, mortality reduction) --> limited
Practical Strategies
  • Use March CRC Awareness Month as springboard for dedicated EOCRC campaigns
  • Share bi-/multilingual posts to broaden reach (especially high-risk/underserved populations)
  • Highlight survivor stories --> humanize EOCRC, encourage earlier symptom evaluation
  • Collaborate with advocacy groups and trainees to co-create culturally relevant content
UVA Campaign Example
  • English- and Spanish-language educational flyers/infographics created
  • Disseminated via social media to ↑ awareness of EOCRC and red-flag symptoms
Strategy 5: Engaging Young People in EOCRC Prevention
  • Engaging teenagers and young adults is vital --> lead-time messaging saves lives
Educational Priorities for Youth
  • Adopt healthy diets (limit sugary-sweetened beverages)
  • Increase physical activity --> primary prevention
  • Recognize and act on red-flag symptoms
  • Knowledge carried home --> promotes timely CRC screening for parents
Engaging Medical Trainees
  • Medical students and residents represent next generation of healthcare providers
  • Can shift public/professional perception to consider CRC diagnosis in young patients
  • Foster long-term commitment to CRC screening and advocacy
  • Spur interest in EOCRC research
Partnering Benefits
  • Youth bring creativity, digital fluency, authenticity
  • Messages resonate with peers and family members
  • Use of social media platforms extends reach of evidence-based information
  • Young adults trust health info from medical providers > celebrities
  • Essential for pairing youth engagement with credible sources
Skills Developed Through Engagement
  • Leadership
  • Communication
  • Social responsibility
Practical Strategies for Gastroenterologists
  • Partner with youth organizations (schools, service clubs, sports teams, fraternities/sororities, medical student groups)
  • Offer community service hours that benefit students and public health
  • Collaborate with educators to integrate EOCRC education into:
  • High school curricula
  • Undergraduate curricula
  • Medical school curricula
  • Engage community partners:
  • Nonprofit organizations
  • Cancer coalitions
  • Local CRC roundtables
Virginia Youth Engagement Examples
High School & Undergraduate Level
  • Hitting Cancer Below the Belt (HCB2): Virginia-based nonprofit led by Melinda Conklin
  • Runs a Junior Board educating high school students on colon health and CRC prevention
  • Members meet monthly to create educational content
  • Plan informational activities
  • Volunteer at events
  • Create "colon clubs" within their high schools
Medical School Level
  • University of Virginia School of Medicine incorporated EOCRC content into first-year pre-clinical curriculum
  • Goals: ↑ EOCRC awareness and improve early symptom recognition
Residents & Fellows Level
  • Virginia Colorectal Cancer Round Table (VCCRT) hosts a "Residents & Fellows Corner"
  • Encourages trainees to present scholarly work on CRC screening and prevention
  • Supports statewide March CRC awareness month activities
Key Takeaway: Coordinated, Sustained Effort Required
  • Effective communication of elevated familial risk to FDRs of CRC/ACP patients
  • Ensuring timely colonoscopy for:
  • Young symptomatic individuals
  • Those with abnormal SBT
  • Leveraging digital tools (social media)
  • Engaging youth in prevention efforts
Implementation Integration
  • All strategies --> readily incorporated into routine gastroenterology practice
  • Multifaceted and collaborative approach essential
  • Gastroenterologists can play pivotal role in mitigating EOCRC within their communities
